content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a training-free approach to estimate the required architecture for each image before denoising which is simple and effective. They explore the correlation between the texture of image and the width and depth of an optimal network prior and utilize it to search an optimal subnetwork for each image. It is the first to associate the architectural design for DIP with the image textures and avoid the early-stopping strategy in DIP.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The proposed idea sounds interesting and the exploration of correlation between the architectural design for DIP and image textures is meaningful.
2.  The proposed work alleviates the burdens of parameter tuning in practice when ground true images are not available

Weaknesses:
1. The novel idea of DIP does not need to provide training set, nor does it require the uncorrupted image as the ground-truth. It uses the network prior to restore the noisy image directly, which has more significance in the real image denoising. However, the authors did not evaluate on the real-world images for demonstration.
2. Lack of description for the denoiser training process after the width and height estimation. It is suggested to provide a framework such as NAS-DIP.
3. Description of “Scoring” in page 6 is not clear enough. The final score refers to the “Texture scores” in Figure 5 and Table 1? If so, why to analyze the texture scores according to dataset, instead of all images since the proposed method is image -specific?
4. Fig. 4 is not cited in the text.
5. How about the robustness of the proposed method to noise level, especially the real noise?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Quality of this paper is general due to the lack of some descriptions such as the denoising training after width and height estimation, even though the clarity is clear for understanding. On the other hand, the experiments degrade the quality of this work, since that they did not evaluate on real noisy images.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed work sounds interesting to explore the correlation between image textures and width and height of network prior for architecture design for each image. It alleviates the burdens of parameter tuning in practice when ground true images are not available, however, they did not conduct experiments on real noisy images. Besides, the texture score is not clearly explained for width estimation, especially across different noise levels, even real noise.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper identifies the depth and width of Deep Image Prior as two main factors of denoising performance. It further links the width to a texture related score based on Power Spectrum Density fall-off rate, Grey Level Co-occurrence Matrix, and image dimensions. Experiments on three datasets show the resulting under-parametrized architectures outperform previous DIP related methods in denoising with a fixed stopping point at 3k iterations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- S1: A more efficient architecture search method and a more limited search space compared to previous works for DIP.
    
- S2: Resulting in lighter architectures in terms of number of params.
    
- W1: Limited to denoising and does not show applicability to a broader set of tasks as do the compared methods.
    
- W2: Lacks a comparison to SOTA denoising methods such as [1,2,3,4], just to mention a few.
    
- W3: Lacks an ablation study showing the importance of each component of the proposed method for width estimation.
    

[1] Wang Z, Cun X, Bao J, Zhou W, Liu J, Li H. Uformer: A general u-shaped transformer for image restoration, CVPR 2022

[2] Liang J, Cao J, Sun G, Zhang K, Van Gool L, Timofte R. Swinir: Image restoration using swin transformer, ICCV 2021

[3] Pang T, Zheng H, Quan Y, Ji H. Recorrupted-to-recorrupted: unsupervised deep learning for image denoising, CVPR 2021

[4] Huang T, Li S, Jia X, Lu H, Liu J. Neighbor2neighbor: Self-supervised denoising from single noisy images, CVPR 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The following concerns impacts the significance and quality of the work:
    
1- As also pointed in W1 and W2, the paper mainly compares against the family of DIP methods that are designed to work for a broad set of applications such as inpainting and super-resolution. However, it is targeted towards a single task of denoising. Unless the experiments are expanded to the same broad set of applications, there is no justification not to compete against state of the art in denoising.
    
2- The paper claims the proposed method does not need early stopping. However, this is only shown for one of the images in the set12 that 3k iterations is probably close to the peak. The ground truth PSNR curve could look completely different for another image in the three considered datasets. In other words, there is not enough evidence to support this claim.
    
3- Table 2 of ISNAS-DIP [5] reports a PSNR of 28.06 for set12 under a /sigma of 25. However, this paper reports a lower number 26.99. What justifies this difference? Could other reported numbers be affected by the same issue in comparisons? For example, could it be that the considered fixed set of hyperparameters such as the learning rate of 0.01 be biased in favor of the proposed method?
    

[5] Arican ME, Kara O, Bredell G, Konukoglu E. ISNAS-DIP: Image-Specific Neural Architecture Search for Deep Image Prior, CVPR 2022
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper shows some improvements for denoising among DIP methods. However, the positioning of the paper among DIP approaches and not showing its performance at least among the usual broad set of tasks for DIP is not justified. Also, more experiments are required to justify the contribution of components and claims. Besides, some clarifications are required with regards to the results.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper empirically observed two key factors that predominantly affect the deep network denoising performance. Based on these findings, a training-free NAS approach is proposed to find optimal architectures for each individual image.  Experiments are performed with competitive performance on CBM3D, CBSD69, and Set12 datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

 1. The paper is well-structured and smooth in writing. 

 2.  These observations are counterintuitive but interesting.

Weakness:

 1. One of the advantages of a deep network is that it can be applied to a wide arrange of images. In contrast, conventional methods often need to optimize energy functions on each specific image. In this paper, an image-specific NAS technique is proposed which aims to provide optimal network architectures for each specific image. It means the network architecture is highly specific and has nearly zero robustness. Although the search for architecture is training-free, we still need a certain amount of time to optimize the searched network. The time and computation complexities should also be considered. Also since the setting is close to conventional methods setting, conventional methods should also be included in the comparison, in terms of accuracy and processing time.

 2. The assumption/ observation made by this paper is dependent on the complexity of images. However, there is no definition or quantitative measurement of this property, i.e., why Lena has lower complexity than Baboon? Also, how to define an image as a fine-grained image or a coarse-grained image? Without a proper definition, the assumptions/findings of the paper cannot be held.

 3. The experiments are not convincing. 
     1). The evaluation is only performed on 3 small datasets with less than 100 images in total. Image denoising is a common low-level vision task and can be easily extended to thousands or millions of images. Whether the findings still hold in general images is yet to be proven. It can be seen that there are some ambiguities in the BSD68 dataset and it only contains 68 images. 
     2). The paper only evaluates the denoising performance of hand-crafted Gaussian white noise. Since this noise is almost distinct from nature images in frequency, the performance of real noise images is yet to be proven. 
     3). What are the PSNR and the SSIM of the noised images? 
     4). As the noise level increases, the performance of the proposed method degenerates faster than competitors. Is that mean the network may have trouble handling large noise?
     5). What are the ground truth widths? How to guarantee they are the optimal widths?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The quality of the paper is OK and the novelty is OK. However, there are several concerns as indicated above.
content.summary_of_the_review:
3 main concerns:

1. The validity of the problem setting. Why do we need a specific network for each image?

2. The definition of image complexity.

3. The experiment is not convincing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The method proposes a training-free approach for estimating the optimal architecture for denoising a given image using Deep Image Prior. Unlike other methods, method a proposes zero-cost and image-dependent architectural design, leading to versatility in the network architecture choice. Due to its underparameterized nature, it relies less on early stopping. The method is also tested on decoder-only architectures. There are two main observations - increased depth (which leads to more downsampling-upsampling layers) leads to more blurriness, and is effective in denoising images with less high frequency textures. The paper makes fourier spectrum analysis of the image to determine the optimal width and depth to use for denoising.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Upsampling layers contributing to most of the denoising effect is an interesting observation, it shows that its necessary and underparameterization is not a solution.
- Paper is written nicely and details are generally very easy to follow.
- Fig.5. is a useful figure - shows that there is a (weak) correlation between the optimal size of the width versus texture/fourier metrics of the image. Although this raises the question: can you use this idea to learn a CNN classifier to predict a multi-class classification task (width).?

Weaknesses:
- Claims about the significant improvements in decoder-only architectures is not well supported with experiments.
- In general, the experimental setup doesn't back up the claims very well. Testing is only done with known levels of Gaussian noise, with $\sigma = 25$ not seeming to add or distort the image significantly at all. 
- Other claims about deeper layers seems questionable. In particular, "we empirically observed that a deeper model (without skip connections) results in increasingly blurry outputs for finer-grained images, while the more homogeneous image is much less affected" - the observation could be due to the downsample-upsample combination increasingly blurring the feature maps. How about deeper layers that do not perform any downsampling-upsampling combination (maintaining spatial size of the features throughout the network).
- The method simply discounts the effect of skip-connections in the Hourglass architectures used the experiments. More specifically, how do skip-connections balance out the effect of (or change the effect rate of) downsampling? What’s the effect of skip connections - How much does it contribute to denoising compared to upsampling? Is there a tradeoff? Skip connections can be put in the more downsampled layers, to change the "effective downsampling rate". 
- The PSD fall off ratio doesn't make sense to me. The choice of ratio of top 25-50% v/s 50-75% of the total energy is very ad-hoc and is not well supported.
- The depth/width estimation method doesn't perform well for a higher noise level compared to other baselines, so I'm not sure if the method is scalable to other noise levels/noise types.

More questions/clarifications:
- The analysis in Sec 3.3.1 picks $d = 2$ for all experiments. How universal is this result? 
- The "search space" of the method is rather small (depth is fixed and only three width choices are available). How does this change with architectural differences - if one uses architectures other than Hourglass or UNet? 
- The paper uses the terms "coarse-grained" and "fine-grained" images. How is this defined mathematically (either using the noisy or clean image in the definition)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear and easy to understand. The feature generation from images to check the correlation with the optimal width of the network is novel, and analysis is done to optimize the network for a per-image basis, which is what DIP was intended for. The work is very clear to understand, and enough details are provided to reproduce this work.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work aims to find a computationally efficient way to determine the optimal depth and width of the hourglass architecture to denoise images. There are several weaknesses in the work - the major of which is no consideration of different types of realistic noise models (i.e. limited experimental setup). Moreover, the family of architectures considered in this work is rather limited - only limiting itself to hourglass networks without skip connections, which lowers the "search space" within the network anyway. The effect of other blocks like skip connections, resnet blocks, normalization layers, etc. is not considered. Therefore, my initial recommendation is a weak reject.

content.title: Faster Neural Architecture "Search" for Deep Image Prior
content.TL;DR: We develop a faster and training-free architecture design strategy to estimate the required architecture for each image in advance.
content.abstract: Deep image prior (DIP) is known for leveraging the spectral bias of the convolutional neural network (CNN) towards lower frequencies in various single-image restoration tasks.  Such inductive bias has been widely attributed to the network architecture. Existing studies therefore either handcraft the architecture or use automated neural architecture search (NAS). However, there is still a lack of understanding on how the architectural choice corresponds to the image to be restored, leading to an excessively large search space that is both time and computationally-expensive for typical NAS techniques. As a result, the architecture is often searched and fixed for the whole dataset, while the best-performing one could be image-dependent. Moreover, common architecture search requires ground truth supervision, which is often not accessible. In this work, we present a simple yet effective \emph{training-free} approach to estimate the required architecture for \emph{every image} in advance. This is motivated by our empirical findings that the width and depth of a good network prior are correlated with the texture of the image, which can be estimated during pre-processings. Accordingly, the design space is substantially shrunk to a handful of subnetworks within a given large network. The experiments on denoising across different noise levels show that a subnetwork with proper setups could be a more effective network prior than the original network while being highly under-parameterized, making it not critically require early-stopping as with the original large network.
